Learning Objectives
Review patellofemoral anatomy.
Describe the history, physical examination, and radiographic evaluation of patients with
patellofemoral injuries.
Summarize the differential diagnosis for patellofemoral pain with an emphasis on
differentiating between patellofemoral laxity, patellofemoral instability, and patellofemoral
pain syndrome.
Recognize that an MRI should be obtained for every patella dislocation event.
Explain why isolated medial patellofemoral ligament reconstruction is the preferred technique
for the management of recurrent patellofemoral instability.

Background
Epidemiology of Patellar Instability
Incidence: 5.8/100,000 in the general population; occurs most commonly in individuals in their
teenage years and twenties.
Incidence: 29/100,000 in individuals aged 10 to 17 years.1
Higher incidence of patellar instability in women2
High rate of recurrence: 15% to 44% after nonsurgical management3
With each subsequent dislocation, 50% risk of recurrence1
More than one-half (55%) of patients fail to return to sports activity after index dislocation
(noncollegiate, nonprofessional)4

Epidemiology of Patellar Instability
Patellofemoral instability is a common orthopaedic problem, affecting between 5
and49/100,000 individuals, with most dislocations occurring in individuals in their
teenage years and twenties.4 Rates of recurrence are high after a first-time dislocation,
ranging from 15% to 44%.2 Female patients have a higher incidence of instability and a
higher rate of recurrent instability after an initial patellar dislocation.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Bony Anatomy
Patellofemoral joint consists of the trochlea and the patella
Trochlear geometry is critical for stability.
Stability is affected by trochlear grove depth, shape, and steepness.
The patella consist of three patellar facets: medial, lateral, and the third (odd facet)

AAOS | Patellofemoral Joint Disorders/Patellofemoral Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004077
2/30

The lateral facet is most superior on the anterior aspect of femur.
The third facet (odd facet) is the smallest facet and is along the medial border.
Trochlea

Trochlea
The trochlea is formed by the anterior aspect of the distal femur and has two facets. The
lateral femoral condyle is 3.4 mm more anterior than the medial femoral condyle in the
axial plane, which results in the lateral facet being larger and extending more proximal
than the medial facet. The lateral wall of the patellofemoral articulation is the primary
osseous restraint to lateral patella translation after the patella is engaged in the groove
during flexion.5 The trochlear groove is a conduit for patella gliding. The trochlear groove
deepens as it moves distally and deviates laterally as it terminates at the femoral notch.
The normal depth of the trochlear groove is 5.2 mm.6 The depth of the trochlear groove
can be measured via the sulcus angle. Trochlear dysplasia is characterized by an
excessively shallow trochlea, with or without asymmetric facets. Trochlear dysplasia may
lead to patellar instability secondary to decreased bony stability between the patella and
trochlea. Trochlear dysplasia has been defined radiographically by Dejour et al.7 A
trochlear prominence greater than 3 mm and a trochlear depth less than 4 mm is
deemed pathologic.
Patella

Patella
The patella is the largest sesamoid bone in the body and lies between the patellar
tendon and the quadriceps tendon. The patella receives its blood supply via an
anastomotic ring surrounding the patella.8,9 It glides within the trochlear groove of the
distal femur. The patellar tendon attaches to the inferior pole of the patella, whereas the
quadriceps tendon attaches to the superior pole. The shape of the patella plays a critical
role in its function and the pathology of the patellofemoral joint. The anterior surface of
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:34 PM
AAOS | Patellofemoral Joint Disorders/Patellofemoral Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004077
3/30

the patella is convex, with an overlaying thin layer of periosteal and retinacular tissue.
The articular surface of the patella is divided by a longitudinal median ridge. Although a
total of seven facets are present on the patella, most patellofemoral pathology occurs in
the primary two facets, the medial and lateral facets. The lateral facet is longer in the
sagittal plane and has a greater slope to match the slope of the lateral femoral condyle.
The medial facet is smaller in surface area and has a greater slope than the lateral facet.
The third facet, or odd facet, is the smallest and most medial facet on the patella. It
articulates with the lateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle with more than 90° of
flexion. The body of the patella has the thickest area of articular cartilage, measuring 7
mm in depth.10 Patellar cartilage has the greatest congruity in the axial plane. This
congruency contributes to the gliding capability of the patellofemoral joint. The cartilage
may not have the same contour as its underlying subchondral bone.11 The inferior pole
of the patella is extra-articular and is not covered by articular cartilage.

Quadriceps
Serves as dynamic stabilizer
Greatest role between 0° and 30° of flexion
Medialis
Deviates 47° from the femoral axis
Lateralis
Deviates 35° from the femoral axis
Vastus medialis obliquus (VMO)
First part of quadriceps to weaken, last to strengthen
Medial soft-tissue structures (Figure 1)
Three layers of the medial knee; together make up the medial patellofemoral complex
Superficial: retinaculum, medial patellotibial ligament
Medial patellotibial ligament has a role in restriction of lateral translation, patellar tilt, and
patellar rotation at 90° of flexion
Intermediate: medial patellofemoral ligament (MPFL)
MPFL
Primary medial stabilizer in the first 30° of flexion
Fibers fan out under the VMO

Medial Patellofemoral Joint

Medial Patellofemoral Joint
The quadriceps tendon inserts at the superior pole of the patella and is a critical dynamic
stabilizer of the patellofemoral joint. It is composed of four muscles: rectus femoris,
vastus medalis, vastus intermedius, and vastus lateralis. These muscles converge to form
the quadriceps tendon 5 to 8 cm superior to the patella. The patellar tendon inserts on
the inferior pole of the patella and has a mean length and width of 4.6 cm and 24 to 33
cm, respectively.14 The patella inserts on the tibial tubercle, slightly lateral to the long
axis of the tibia. The medial soft-tissue complex of the patellofemoral joint is composed
of the VMO, MPFL, medial patellotibial ligament, and the medial retinaculum. These
structures play a critical role in dynamic patellar stability. The VMO is the primary
dynamic restraint to lateral translation of the patella.10 VMO weakness has been
demonstrated to result in lateral patella instability between 0° and 15° of flexion.
Therefore, VMO strengthening is critical during rehabilitation of patellofemoral
instability.13,15 The MPFL is the primary passive restraint to lateral patella translation.
The MPFL contributes to as much as 60% of lateral translation restraint at 0° and 30° of
knee flexion.
Lateral Patellofemoral Joint


Lateral Patellofemoral Joint
The lateral soft-tissue complex of the patella is composed of multiple layers but can be
divided into the superficial and deep layers. The superficial layer is composed of the
oblique lateral retinaculum, whereas the deep layer is made up of the oblique and
transverse fibers, specifically the patellotibial and epicondylopatellar bands.6 The lateral
retinaculum serves as an important secondary restraint to the patella. Iatrogenic release
of the lateral soft-tissue restraints may worsen patellar instability, especially patients
with deficient medial patella restraints.
Mechanism of Injury
Patellar dislocation may result from direct or indirect mechanisms of injury.
Direct = direct blow to the knee/patella
Indirect = pivoting force with external rotation of the tibia in near full extension (noncontact)
Native anatomy influencing stability
Trochlear dysplasia
Mechanism: less bony constraint to lateral patella translation
Patellar height
Patella alta is associated with recurrent dislocation.
Mechanism: greater knee flexion is required for the patella to engage with the trochlea,
predisposing patients to instability in early flexion.
Can have concomitant trochlear dysplasia, resulting in increased instability
Increased quadriceps angle = greater laterally directed force on the patella and increased
instability
Genu valgum
VMO weakness or atrophy: less medial dynamic force
MPFL insufficiency: loss of primary static stabilizer to lateral translation
Femoral anteversion
External tibial torsion
Generalized hyperlaxity
Patellofemoral Pathoanatomy


Patellofemoral Pathoanatomy
Patellofemoral gliding relies on an interplay of osseous, static, and dynamic soft-tissue
structures. Abnormalities of bony or soft-tissue structures may lead to maltracking,
which may predispose patients to instability. Normal patellofemoral tracking proceeds
through the patella, which acts to increase the mechanical advantage of the extensor
mechanism. By increasing the moment arm of the quadriceps, the patella decreases the
amount of force required for knee extension.10 In full extension, minimal posterior
directed force is present on the patella, which rests in a slightly lateral position in the
trochlear groove. From 0° to 30° of flexion, the primary restraint to lateral translation is
the MPFL. As the knee begins flexion, the patella begins to track medially and engages
the trochlear groove. At 20° to 30° of flexion, the patella is engaged in the trochlear
groove, which confers stability. As flexion progress to 60°, the contact area of the patella
increases and moves from distal to proximal. As knee flexion proceeds to 90°, increasing
posterior directed force is placed on the patella by the increasing tension of the
quadriceps tendon. Given the bony stability afforded with deeper knee flexion, near full
extension is associated with a higher risk for instability. During a dislocation episode, the
knee typically is in near full extension and an external rotation force is applied to the
tibia and foot. The patient may feel the patella move out of place and contract the
quadriceps tendon to pull the patella back into the groove. Trochlear dysplasia (less
bony constraint), patella alta (greater flexion required for bony engagement), an
increased quadriceps angle (greater lateral pull of the patella), or inadequate medial
support via dynamic (VMO) or static (MPFL) means leads to a greater risk of instability.
Evaluation and Diagnosis
Patient History and Physical Examination
A thorough patient history is critical to identify the mechanism of injury, prior injuries, and risk
factors.
Physical examination
Standing position


Radiography
After a detailed patient history and physical examination, a series of plain radiographs
should be obtained if indicated. This series should include bilateral weight-bearing AP
and Rosenberg views, a lateral view of the affected knee, and a bilateral low-flexion
(Merchant) view.19,20 Femoral anteversion will be present on an AP view of the tibia and
an oblique view of the distal femur. A lateral view is critical because it allows for
evaluation of patella alta or baja, trochlear dysplasia, and patellar tilt. Mechanical axis
radiographs allow for evaluation of coronal plane tibiofemoral malalignment and lateral
femoral condyle hypoplasia.21
Sagittal Alignment

9/3/26, 5:34 PM
AAOS | Patellofemoral Joint Disorders/Patellofemoral Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004077


Sagittal Alignment
Patella alta results from a proximal position of the patella in relation to the trochlear
groove and/or the patellar tendon. As a result, a greater flexion angle is required for the
patella to engage in the trochlear groove, which produces a greater arc of motion in
which the patella can become unstable. Patella baja occurs if the patella rests well below
the trochlea and results in increased joint reactive force. An increase in joint reactive
force may result in chondromalacia, patellofemoral pain syndrome, and accelerated
patellofemoral osteoarthritis. Patella baja often results from previous soft-tissue
realignment procedures that do not effectively manage the underlying pathology. The
preferred measurement for sagittal alignment is the Caton-Deschamps ratio, which is
measured on a lateral radiograph. The Caton-Deschamps ratio is calculated by dividing
the distance between the most distal edge of the articular surface of the patella and the
superior/anterior edge of the tibia and the articular length of the patella. A Caton-
Deschamps ratio greater than 1.2 is associated with patella alta, whereas a Caton-
Deschamps ratio less than 0.6 is diagnostic of patella baja.22 The Caton-Deschamps ratio
offers a distinct advantage over other systems because it will change if the patient has
undergone a distalizing procedure.6

Able to measure tibial tuberosity–trochlear groove (TT-TG) distance; MRI may underestimate

Evaluate for chondral injuries
Evaluate for osteochondral fracture, loose bodies
Evaluate for concomitant ligament or meniscal injuries
Assess for bone bruise patterns
Characteristic bruising on the medial patellar facet and the lateral femoral condyle


Advanced Imaging Studies
Cross-sectional imaging allows for evaluation of two relationships that are critical to
better define patellofemoral anatomy. These ratios are the TT-TG distance and the tibial
tubercle–posterior cruciate ligament (TT-PCL) distance. These values are calculated by
superimposing two images: one at the deepest aspect of the trochlea and another
through the center of the tibial tuberosity on axial views. The TT-TG distance is used to
define the medial to lateral offset of the patella in the trochlear groove. Normal TT-TG
distance ranges from 9 to 16 mm on CT scans and 9 to 13 mm on MRIs, with values
greater than 15 mm indicative of an increased risk of patellar instability.7,23,24 Values
greater than 20 mm represent excessive lateralization of the tibial tubercle and are
associated with an increased incidence of patellar instability.25 The TT-TG distance is
affected by the screw-home mechanism of the knee and by abnormal trochlear
morphology. Therefore, the TT-PCL distance has gained popularity. The TT-PCL distance
is the ratio between the tibial tubercle and the medial border of the posterior cruciate
ligament. This is measured on two axial images that produce the best view of the medial
posterior cruciate ligament tibial attachment and the trajectory line parallel to the dorsal
tibial condylar line. The mean TT-PCL distance is 11.9 (± 4.67 mm), with values greater
than 20 mm considered pathologic.26,27
Differential Diagnosis
A wide spectrum of conditions may lead to patellofemoral disorders.
Anterior knee pain is not exclusively caused by patellofemoral disorders and may be a result of
patellofemoral pain syndrome.
Patellofemoral pain syndrome: nonspecific diagnosis without overt patellar instability;
anterior knee pain associated with running, climbing, prolonged sitting, and/or a maintained
flexed knee position
Patellofemoral disorders can be broadly divided into six categories:28
Traumatic
Acute trauma: direct anterior blow to the knee
Fracture of the patella, trochlea, or tibial tubercle
Rupture of the quadriceps or patellar tendon

Management
Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome
Nonspecific diagnosis without overt patellar instability. Anterior knee pain that is associated
with running, climbing, prolonged sitting, and/or a maintained flexed knee position
Nonsurgical management is the main treatment option. Physical therapy/exercises
emphasizing quadriceps, core, and hip musculature strengthening
Predictors of successful nonsurgical management include negative patellar tilt, a TT-TG
distance of less than 14.6 mm, no patellar chondral defects, short duration of symptoms, and
high quadriceps cross-sectional area.29
Additional proposed modalities include patellar bracing/taping.
No single treatment algorithm has been described as beneficial for nonspecific patellofemoral
pain syndrome.30
Surgical management rarely is indicated for isolated patellofemoral pain syndrome.
SEND FEEDBACK

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004077
17/30


Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome
Patellofemoral pain syndrome, also termed patella chondromalacia or patellofemoral
syndrome, is a nonspecific term used to classify anterior knee pain in the absence of
patellar instability.30 Patellofemoral pain syndrome typically is associated with anterior
knee pain that is worse with loaded flexion activities, such as running, climbing, and
squatting, and with prolonged flexed knee positions. Although multiple potential causes
of anterior knee pain exist, it is often a multifactorial etiology. In addition, the diagnostic
workup should include an attempt to identify an underlying pathologic process and
direct management toward the underlying etiology. After other anatomic and
biomechanic considerations are excluded, patients typically are treated nonsurgically,
which includes physical therapy and bracing and/or taping. Some evidence supports the
use of hip and core modalities in patients with patellofemoral pain because they may
lead to greater strength gains and earlier resolution of symptoms.31 In addition, a
systematic review identified predictors of successful nonsurgical management to include
negative patellar tilt, a normal TT-TG distance, the absence of chondral defects, a short
duration of symptoms, and a high quadriceps cross-sectional area.29 A more recent
systematic review found that no single treatment modality was clinically successful in the
treatment of all patients with patellofemoral pain.30 This emphasizes the importance of
a thorough patient history and physical examination to provide individualized
nonsurgical treatment to patients with patellofemoral pain.
Patellar Instability
Nonsurgical Management
Closed reduction of the dislocation (usually occurs spontaneously); management via NSAIDs,
activity modifications, and physical therapy
Nonsurgical management is the main treatment option for most first-time dislocations.
Contraindications to nonsurgical management include large intra-articular loose bodies or
large reparable osteochondral fragments.
MRI should be obtained in patients with an acute dislocation to evaluate for osteochondral
fracture and loose bodies and/or to aid in risk stratification and patient counseling.

Physical therapy consists of strengthening and stretching from core to floor, including closed-
chain exercises, quadriceps strengthening and VMO strengthening exercises, patellar
taping/bracing, and hip and core strengthening.
Aspiration may be considered for a tense hemarthrosis. The presence of fat globules within
the serosanguineous fluid is indicative of a fracture.
Recurrent dislocation rates range from 15% to 44%.

Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management is the main treatment option for first-time patellar
dislocations. Patellar dislocations typically automatically reduce after dislocation. If the
patella does not automatically reduce, reduction maneuvers should be performed.
These maneuvers consist of extension of the knee via a medially directed force to the
patella. During the time of relocation, the patient is at risk of osteochondral injury,
typically originating from the medial facet of the patella and/or the lateral femoral
condyle. If these are identified on plain radiographs or axial MRIs, then acute surgical
management with arthroscopic removal or repair should be considered.32 In the
absence of intra-articular bodies or osteochondral defects, most dislocations are
managed nonsurgically. This consists of early weight-bearing modifications, NSAIDs for
pain relief, physical therapy with an emphasis on core to floor and quadriceps/VMO
strengthening, and a gradual return to activity.31,33 The focus of nonsurgical
management is reducing knee stress, balancing musculature forces, and increasing
dynamic stability and musculature control. All patients should be risk stratified to
identify their risk for recurrent instability because many studies have demonstrated a
high rate of recurrent instability after index dislocation.34,35 Risk factors for recurrent
instability include age younger than 16 years or skeletal immaturity, contralateral
instability, trochlear dysplasia, patella alta, TT-TG distance greater than 16 mm, and
patellar tilt greater than 20o.34,35,36 Outcomes after nonsurgical management vary in the
literature. Nonsurgical management is associated with good patient-reported outcome
scores but not normal scores, with Kujala scores and Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis
Outcome Scores (KOOS) reaching a maximum of 82.7% and 86.3%, respectively.37 In
addition, a meta-analysis reported a 31% pooled redislocation.37

Surgical Management
Indications include acute intra-articular loose bodies, large reparable osteochondral
fragments, and recurrent instability. Relative indications include first-time dislocation with a
high risk for recurrent instability and patients with a concomitant knee injury.
Treatment options include MPFL reconstruction with or without a concomitant bony
procedure (ie, tibial tubercle osteotomy, rotational osteotomy, trochleoplasty). MPFL
reconstruction often is performed in isolation but may require concomitant procedures based
on the patient pathology and anatomy.
MPFL primary repair is associated with an increased risk of recurrent dislocation compared
with MPFL reconstruction.
Isolated lateral retinaculum release is ineffective in the management of patellar instability. The
lateral retinaculum is a secondary stabilizer to lateral translation. Isolated release may
exacerbate and worsen patella instability. Lateral retinaculum release or lengthening may be
utilized as an adjunct to other stabilization procedures, especially if fixed patellar tilt and
lateral retinaculum tightness prevent centering the patella on the trochlea.
MPFL Reconstruction
The MPFL is the primary restraint to pathologic lateral translation of the patella and serves as a
checkrein for lateral translation, making it the essential lesion in patellar instability.
Reconstruction is commonly performed with the use of autograft or allograft. Either gracilis or
semitendinosus is commonly used, both of which are stronger than the native MPFL.
The MPFL originates on the superomedial aspect of the medial border of the patella and
courses medially along the distal border of the VMO anterior to the medial joint capsule. The
femoral insertion is between the adductor magnus tendon and the superficial medial collateral
ligament.
Fluoroscopic landmarks can be used to verify femoral and patellar positioning. Anatomy and
isometry assessments also are useful to ensure anatomic graft positioning.
MPFL reconstruction is associated with good patient-reported outcomes, high levels of return
to sports activity, and low rates of recurrent dislocation.

The MPFL serves as the primary soft-tissue restraint to pathologic lateral patella
translation, making it the essential lesion to address during surgical management. MPFL
repair or medial soft-tissue imbrication has been associated with inferior results and
higher rates of recurrent instability compared with MPFL reconstruction.38 Therefore,
the trend has been in favor of MPFL reconstruction with the use of graft. Various
techniques for MPFL reconstruction have been described.39 Good to excellent results
have been reported after MPFL reconstruction, with low recurrent dislocation rates. In a
series of 211 patients who underwent isolated MPFL reconstruction, Kujala patient-
reported outcome scores improved from 56.1 to 88.8, with a 4.7% failure rate.40 Return
to sports activity rates have been excellent, with studies reporting as much as a 100%
return to sports activity after MPFL reconstruction, with 53% to 84% returning to the
same level of activity40-42 (Video 1).

Indications include lateral retinaculum tightness and lateral patella compression syndrome
and to allow for soft-tissue balancing in patients with instability; not indicated as isolated
procedure for the management of patellar instability.43
Lateral retinaculum lengthening is performed in an open fashion and affords adjustment in
lateral translation to allow for balanced patellar tracking.
Avoids medial patellar instability and over-release
If performed in combination with a tibial tubercle osteotomy, should be re-approximated
after fixation of the tibial tubercle osteotomy
Lateral retinaculum release can be performed via open or arthroscopic means, and various
techniques have been described. Care should be taken to avoid cutting the vastus lateralis
tendon because this may cause iatrogenic instability.28
Complications include medial patellar instability, muscle atrophy, and pain.
Tibial Tubercle Osteotomy
Indications include recurrent instability with an increased TT-TG distance, typically greater than
20 mm; patella alta; a Caton-Deschamps ratio greater than 1.4; and/or need to unload
cartilage defects.
Altering the angle of the cut or transferring the tubercle proximally or distally may lead to a
different effect on patellofemoral stability and patellofemoral joint cartilage loading.
Direct medial tibial tubercle transfer can be performed in patients who have patellar instability
without chondrosis to manage an increased TT-TG distance.
Anterior tibial transfer will tilt the patella, shift the primary contact area proximally, and off-
load the distal patellar cartilage. It should be avoided in patients with proximal patella
chondral lesions.
Anteromedial transfer can be performed to decrease the TT-TG distance and off-load distal
and lateral chondral defects.
The tibial tubercle can be distalized to manage extreme patella alta in patients with patellar
instability or to unload distal patella chondral lesions. Distalization is associated with a higher
complication profile than anteromedialization because an unhinged osteotomy is associated
with higher rates of delayed union.44

A tibial tubercle osteotomy alters the distal insertional anatomy of the patella at the
tibial tubercle. Various procedures have been described, including direct medialization
(Elmslie-Trillat), anteromedialization (Fulkerson), and anteriorization (Maquet)
osteotomies. These osteotomies typically rely on a distal intact hinge, performing a
greenstick fracture distally. The osteotomy also can be distalized to manage patella alta.
If including a distalizing component, a complete osteotomy is necessary, which is
associated with a higher risk for delayed union.44 These procedures often are performed
in combination with proximal soft-tissue procedures, such as lateral release or
lengthening and medial repair or reconstruction. A study of 34 athletes demonstrated
excellent results, with a 94% rate of return to sports activity and a mean Lysholm Knee
Scale scores of 91.8 after anteromedialization with lateral release, including distalization
in patients with patella alta.45 Similarly, good to excellent outcomes were reported in
79.2% of patients 4 years after direct medialization osteotomy; however, this decreased
to 62.5% at a mean follow-up of 12 years.46
Trochleoplasty
Indications include severe trochlear dysplasia, with differing techniques based on the type of
dysplasia.47
Contraindicated in patients with patellofemoral arthritis or anterior knee pain without
instability
Typically, not performed in isolation; performed in combination with other bony and/or soft-
tissue procedures. Trochleoplasty rarely is performed as a primary procedure in the United
States.
Can be performed in select patients with open physes without femoral growth disturbances48
Complications
Medial patellofemoral arthritis or medial instability
Typically results from overcorrection or over-tensioning the graft, extensive lateral release
Recurrent instability or recurrent apprehension
Recurrence rates less than 5% with surgical stabilization
Tunnel malpositioning with MPFL reconstruction

Pediatric Special Considerations
Principles are largely the same for pediatric patients; however, in skeletally immature patients,
the MPFL femoral insertion is close to the distal femoral physis.
Inconsistent reports of the location of the MPFL insertion in relation to the physis49-51
Incidence is 41 per 100,000 children and adolescents1
Redislocation rates in pediatric patients have been as high as 70%.52
Alternative fixation methods may be used to avoid physeal injury.
Fixation to the adductor tendon or the periosteum
Fixation distal to the physis, with the tunnel aimed distal and anterior, using fluoroscopy to
verify physis location before drilling
Pediatric-specific techniques may be used as adjuncts to MPFL reconstruction.53
Longitudinal patellar split, with the lateral half rerouted beneath the medial half to medialize
the force vector (Roux-Goldthwait)
Soft-tissue distal patella tendon transfer and periosteal suturing
Guided growth may be considered in patients with genu valgum.
Nonsurgical management is the main treatment option, with a 62% success rate in adolescent
patients.54
Given the high risk of recurrence, early surgical treatment may be considered in the young
adolescent population, especially those who are skeletally immature and younger than 15
years34,35,36 (Video 2).
